entries.title: Anchor the rail's footer and scroll only the stage list

blocks.text: "+ Add stage" and the running totals sat at the end of the rail's flow, so a long exercise pushed them off the bottom of the window. Twenty-three stages made adding a twenty-fourth unreachable without scrolling to the end first.

The rail no longer scrolls: the exercise's details stay at the top, the stage list takes the space left over and scrolls inside it, and the add button and totals are pinned below it with a rule between.

That only works if the rail has a definite height, and it did not. style.css gives body min-height:100vh, which is a floor, not a ceiling — the body grew to fit the content and every "take the rest of the space" child grew with it, measured at 2010px of body in a 733px window. This page is an app shell rather than a document, so body now takes the viewport exactly and hides its own overflow; the panes inside do the scrolling.

That was my doing: the old layout subtracted the nav height with a calc, which gave a definite height by accident. Replacing the calc with flex fixed a nav that was the wrong height and quietly removed the ceiling at the same time.
Checked in a real browser at 1400x820 and at 700x900, where the rail stacks above the workspace and keeps its footer.

entries.title: Colour a stage by what each part of it is

blocks.text: Every field in the workspace looked the same whatever it held, so a stage read as one undifferentiated column of boxes.

The format already has a colour language and the guide has been teaching it in its syntax badges all along: "!" directives amber, "# discussion" green, "?" questions purple, the stage itself in the accent. The builder now uses the same values — the label takes the colour, the controls take a tint of it at rest and the full colour with a soft ring on focus, and the label carries the directive it stands for, so the colour is teaching the format rather than decorating the page.

Facilitator prompts take amber rather than green: they are a "#" list like discussion points, but they are the half of the stage the room never sees, and the guide badges them amber for the same reason.
This sits inside the audience split rather than replacing it. The zone rail still says who sees this; the field now says what it is.
One test pins the two files together: the tokens here must equal the colours the guide's badges use, because two documents claiming to teach the same language is only true while the values match.

entries.title: Reprocess the gallery photographs at 75% rather than 50%

blocks.text: 704x384 was comfortable inline but soft if a picture was ever asked to fill the participant screen. At 1056x576 a full-width insert lands close to native on a 1280px display, and at the default 60% scale there is real detail to spare.

Same settings otherwise: metadata stripped, progressive, 4:2:0, quality 78. 1.0MB becomes 2.0MB across nineteen photographs, the largest 134KB, which stays well inside the 200KB the gallery test holds them to.

entries.title: Replace the gallery photographs with the generated set

blocks.text: New direction: the photographs now come from lib/exercise_data/temp/, generated outside the project, so nothing in the gallery has a third-party licence attached and the machinery built to manage that is no longer needed.

Out: the fourteen drawn scenes and tools/build-scenes.js; the eleven CC0 photographs; both CREDITS.md files and credits.json; tools/fetch-stock.js and its subject lists. build-gallery.js no longer reads credits or writes licence, author and source into the manifest, and the picker no longer draws a credit line under each thumbnail or a licence footnote under the grid.

In: nineteen photographs, named for what they show — an A&E entrance with an ambulance on the bay, a data centre aisle, a comms cabinet, a contact centre, a service desk, an analyst's desk, an open-plan office, an office after hours, a lone workstation at night, a boardroom empty and a board meeting in progress, a planning workshop, council offices, a civic building, an office building, a motorway with freight, a telecoms mast, a power station, and a police car on a residential street.

Halved to 704x384, stripped of metadata, progressive, 4:2:0, quality 78. Checked against quality 92 at 1:1 before settling: no visible difference at the size these are shown. 16MB of source becomes 1.1MB, between 32KB and 65KB each.

The gallery test now checks what still matters — that the manifest and the folders agree in both directions, that labels read as names rather than as generator filenames, that nothing exceeds 200KB, and that no trace of the credit machinery is left in the picker.

entries.title: Draw the scenes rather than licensing them

blocks.text: Sixteen of the twenty-seven photographs were CC BY or CC BY-SA. That obligation does not stop at this repository: it follows every copy of every scenario anyone downloads, and lands on a facilitator who never agreed to it and has no way of knowing. Removed.

They are replaced by fourteen drawn scenes in lib/exercise_data/scenes/, built by tools/build-scenes.js — an ambulance, a fire appliance, a police car, an articulated lorry, a high street, a hospital, a supermarket, a production floor, a data hall, a rack, an office floor, a treatment works, transmission lines and the brick substation on the corner of every British estate.

Generated imagery was considered and is not obviously safer: the training-data question is unsettled, outputs can reproduce protected material, and provider terms vary and change. Drawing them removes the problem rather than exchanging it, because there is no third party in the file.

They are schematic on purpose. A tabletop needs a picture that says "this is a hospital" in the two seconds before anyone reads the stage text, and the British detail that matters is cheap to draw: battenburg markings, a DANGER OF DEATH sign, a parade of shopfronts. One dusk palette across all fourteen, so a gallery of them looks like a set. 208KB for the lot.

Eleven photographs remain, every one public domain or CC0. The picker now says so per category, and the test that used to check credits reached the picker checks the stronger thing instead: that no picture anywhere in the gallery needs crediting at all.

entries.title: Review the stock photographs for date, relevance and Britishness

blocks.text: The first pass took whatever a licence-filtered search returned. Read back against the Commons categories and EXIF, that meant a US ambulance, a Japanese classroom, a Kenyan call centre, a Baghdad control room from 2003 and a reactor panel from 1979 — in a library whose scenarios are set in British councils, NHS trusts and UK suppliers.

fetch-stock.js now reports the country and year of every candidate, read off the categories and EXIF, and a subject can ask for British results first and for period pieces to be left out. Neither rules anything out; they decide what gets looked at first, because the judgement still has to be made by eye.

Six replaced with British equivalents: a yellow-and-green ambulance, a supermarket, an articulated lorry on a motorway, pylons over farmland, Claymills sewage works, a UK production floor. Five added: a fire crew at an incident, West Midlands Police, a high street, Leicester General Hospital, and the little brick substation on the corner of every British estate.

Five dropped. The 1979 reactor panel and the 2003 Baghdad control room were period pieces; the Kenyan call centre and a 2013 desk flat-lay were redundant with better images; the aircraft assembly line was replaced by a UK factory.

The classroom is dropped rather than replaced. Every modern freely-licensed classroom on Commons is a close-up of identifiable children, which does not belong in a stock gallery and certainly not on screen in an exercise about a data breach. CREDITS.md says so, along with the other thing that could not be found — a British office interior — so the gaps read as decisions rather than oversights.

27 photographs, 12 of them British, none from before 2008 except a rack of patch cables which is marked timeless with a reason, since cable does not visibly age. Tests hold the dates, the proportion, and that the exemptions are explicit.

entries.title: Fill the image gallery: 27 photographs and 13 drawn artefacts

blocks.text: The gallery had icons and three phishing screenshots. It now has 58 images across five categories.

Photographs come from Wikimedia Commons via tools/fetch-stock.js, which filters on licence and downloads candidates for review rather than installing them — the search cannot tell a server room from a bicycle rack, both match "rack", and 79 candidates were looked at to choose 27.

Twenty are CC0 or public domain and owe nothing. Seven are CC BY or CC BY-SA, and they are here because the subjects a cyber exercise most needs — a data hall, an office floor, a production line — barely exist under a free licence; searching for them returns 1960s archive photography instead. The credit for those has to travel, so it does: recorded in credits.json, carried into gallery.json by the build, and shown in amber in the picker at the moment someone chooses the picture rather than buried in a file nobody opens. Unsplash, Pexels and Pixabay were not used — their licences forbid redistributing photographs as a collection, which is what a gallery is.

The screenshots, documents and diagrams are drawn, by tools/build-artefacts.js, because no stock library sells a ransom note, a SIEM console, a fraudulent invoice or an escalation chart. Being SVG they stay sharp on a projector, weigh four kilobytes, carry no licence, and the words inside them are editable text — an author can put their own system names in one without redrawing it. Names are generic and placeholders are written as [like this], because an exercise about your finance system is better served by a screen that says FINANCE SYSTEM than by one carrying an invented company nobody recognises.

build-gallery.js now reads a category's credits.json and refuses to let a credited category hide an uncredited file. Ten tests hold the terms: every photograph documented, nothing unredistributable, no CC BY without someone to credit, the credit reaching the picker, the artefacts self-contained and byte-identical to what the generator produces.

entries.title: Reorder the guide into the order people do things

blocks.text: Library, builder, running the room, what came of it — then the format at the end as a reference. The TTXF structure and Markdown sections sat between creating a scenario and running one, which put three hundred lines of syntax in front of anyone reading the page straight through, describing a thing most readers will never type.

The move is a pure reorder: the two sections are byte-identical, only their position changed. The contents list follows, with the reference half marked off under its own label so it reads as somewhere to look things up rather than somewhere to get to.

The pointer into it changed with the move — the format is now "set out in full at the end of this page" rather than "the rest of this page", and someone happy in the builder is told they never need to go there rather than to skip ahead.
Two tests hold the order: the page's headings against the expected sequence, and the contents list against the page.

entries.title: Make the guide lead with the builder, not the file format

blocks.text: The guide introduced TTXF first and mentioned the builder at the bottom as a convenience. That is backwards now: nobody has to touch the format to build a complete exercise, and most people should not.

"Creating and Modifying Scenarios" now opens with the Exercise Builder and what it gives you — the running order with its timing bars, the on-screen/your-notes split, editing the stage as the room will read it, the live participant view, the problem list, and the two ways out. The format follows under "The file underneath", framed as what to read if you want to edit by hand, understand what the builder produces, or diff two versions of an exercise — with an explicit invitation to skip it.

Two things the guide said were no longer true. Validation is not "a strip above the preview"; it is a count beside the title that lists what is wrong and takes you to the stage. And the answer presets are a "Preset" dropdown, not an "Answers" one — the old builder's name.

A test now reads the guide against the page: every control it names by label must exist in editor.html, the builder must be introduced before the syntax, and nothing may describe the builder that was replaced.

entries.title: Make the rebuilt builder usable: editing in place, and a pass over the chrome

blocks.text: Everything since the swap, in one go. Four of these were faults that lost an author's work silently rather than complaining.
Data loss, fixed:

items: Discussion points and prompts were textareas, but the format writes each as "+ text" on one line. A newline went into the file as a line with no directive above it, the parser dropped it, and everything after the break was gone. They are text inputs, which cannot hold one.

An artefact, news frame or picture inserted at a caret was nested inside the paragraph by execCommand, where htmlToSource — which reads top-level children — saw a paragraph and wrote it back as flat prose. The paragraph is split and the block placed between the halves.

A line break typed into an artefact left a
or a
, both of which textContent renders as nothing. Both are read as newlines now.

The .btn family was defined inside the builder this page replaced and went with it, so nine buttons had been rendering as raw browser defaults since the swap. A test now fails on any button class with no rule behind it.

blocks.text: Editing in place. Pictures honour their scale and can be dragged to resize, with arrow keys and a percentage that resets. News headlines, their flags and artefact labels are typed into where they sit rather than deleted and re-inserted — htmlToSource reads a .SFpre-label element in preference to the attribute, which extends what the module accepts without changing what markdown() emits. Every block carries a remove button, because a picture is not text and backspace does not obviously apply to it.

The participant view keeps up: sends are held until the document says it is ready, and coalesced into a frame so a burst of keystrokes is one refresh carrying the latest state rather than ten carrying nine stale ones. The test enumerates twelve ways of changing an exercise and fails on any that is silent.

Accessibility, audited rather than eyeballed: the page had no headings at all, two unnamed controls, eighteen fields labelled only by placeholder, unnamed landmarks, and a picker that left focus behind it. Ten tests now hold that line. --text-muted measures 2.3-2.5:1 on every ground in this palette, so the label token the gym added for that reason moves into style.css and the builder uses it.

Consistency with the gym: the rail is --surface at --sidebar-width, not --mid at 232px, and section labels match. Sharing that token immediately collapsed the layout, because a var() that resolves to nothing invalidates the whole declaration and style.css had been cached for months without it — hence a fallback, a version on the stylesheet, and a test for structural properties that depend on another file.

Also: the opening and the debrief sit in the running order rather than behind two buttons labelled with an ellipsis; a stage has room to write in; Source opens at the height of the field it replaces and grows to its content; "Run it" is "Preview in TTX Gym"; the page calls itself "Exercise Builder", as the navigation always has.
835 tests, up from 780.

entries.title: Swap editor.html for the rebuilt builder

blocks.text: builder.html becomes editor.html and the page it replaces is gone. The URL does not change, so the site nav on four pages, the library's Customise button, the canonical and og:url all keep working untouched; the old page's title, description and card metadata were carried across whole.

Anyone with unfinished work open on the day of the swap would have arrived at an empty page with their scenario still in the browser under the old draft key and no way to reach it. That draft is adopted once, saved under the new key, and the old key released. Rubbish under it is ignored rather than crashing the page.

Two faults the swap exposed, both from the page moving one directory level in the site: %news() had no backdrop, because the renderer points at a path authored relative to gym/ and only the old page corrected it; and the news strap was styled by tag rather than by the class the format emits.

Test suites moved with the pages. test-editor.js tested a page that no longer exists and is retired; test-builder.js took its name, after porting the two groups worth keeping — the one that fails if any construct the renderer can emit has no rule in the stylesheet the author is looking at, and the guide table check. Stage counts, planned length and unreadable durations are re-covered against the new outline foot.

test-parity.js compared two builders and there is now one; it is test-handoff.js, keeping the corpus round trip and the ways in and out. The two-builder comparison over all 39 scenarios is preserved at 5007bbc, the last commit where both pages existed.

entries.title: Close the gaps parity testing found in the rebuilt builder

blocks.text: tests/test-parity.js pushes all 39 shipped scenarios through both builders and compares the exercise the gym would run, rather than the bytes, which the two format differently. All 39 agree, and both agree with the file they were given.
Comparing features rather than output found four things the rebuild simply did not have, all of which would have broken on the day of the swap:

items: no site navigation, so the page could not be left
no ?load=, so the library's Customise button had nowhere to land
no way to hand the scenario to the gym
no control for "! image:", which was carried through load and save but could only be set by hand in Source

blocks.text: Stage reordering the old builder did with up/down buttons. Those are here, and the outline rows are draggable too, which is the natural gesture for a list that is also the map. Duplicating a stage deep-copies its questions; a shared array would have two stages editing the same answers.

Two repairs came with it. The old builder subtracts a 56px nav from the viewport while the nav is 80px tall, so its workspace always ran past the bottom of the window; body is already a flex column, so the new layout takes what is left. And a restored draft now says where it came from and offers a way to start again.

entries.title: Give the builder problem reporting, file drop and the image picker

blocks.text: Problems were reported against line numbers in a file the author never sees. Each is now attributed to the stage it is in — the model is serialised to be checked, and every "@ " line maps a parser line number back to a stage — listed under the status chip, clickable to go there, and flagged in the outline. Warnings are counted separately from errors: a builder that cries breakage over a missing author line teaches people to ignore it.

A .ttxf can be dropped anywhere on the page or opened from the button, and is parsed before it is accepted. A file with no stages is refused by name rather than replacing an hour of work with an empty scenario, replacing real work asks first, and a file that parses with complaints opens the problems list.

The Image button opened with a hard-coded warning icon in it; it now opens the categorised gallery and lands a real image in the WYSIWYG field. The authored "../lib/…" path is kept in data-src so the picture loads here without the rewritten path reaching the file.
insertBlock called document.execCommand with no fallback, so on an engine without it the insert buttons did nothing at all. It now appends the block.

entries.title: Let htmlToSource keep the authored path when display needs another

blocks.text: Scenario media is authored relative to gym/, so an editor that renders it in place may have to load the picture from one path while writing another to the file. Served from a domain root the two look the same, because ".." past the root is clamped — which is why this is easy to miss, and why it breaks only from file:// or a project subpath.

Converting rendered DOM back to .ttxf now reads data-src in preference to src, so an editor can display a working path without rewriting the authored one into the scenario. Falls back to src when there is no data-src, which is every existing caller.

entries.title: Show the real participant window in the builder, picture-in-picture

blocks.text: The builder drew its own miniature of the room screen from the payload fields. It now embeds the participant document itself — the one js/participant-view.js serves to the gym — in a scaled iframe, so there is nothing left to drift.

It floats over the workspace rather than taking a column, because the screen is 16:9 and a column is the wrong shape for it: draggable by its header, resizable from the corner grip or the arrow keys, collapsible to its header, and clamped back into view after every change so it cannot be stranded off-screen with its own handle out of reach. Size and position persist.
Scenario media is written relative to gym/, the builder sits one level up, and a blob-origin iframe can resolve neither, so every img src is made absolute before it crosses.

The panel chrome is written here rather than shared with the gym's mirror, which is tied to eight functions of its own — theme relay, viewport state, sendToParticipants. The part where fidelity matters, the document, is shared.

entries.title: Extract the participant window into js/participant-view.js

blocks.text: The participant document lived inside gym/index.html as a 455-line template literal. Nothing else could use it without copying it, so the builder drew its own miniature of the room screen — a second renderer that could agree with the model while disagreeing with what participants actually saw.

It now lives in js/participant-view.js as the global PRESENTATION_HTML, loaded by the gym and available to any page that wants to show the real thing. The media-sizing script it inlines moves to TTXF.MEDIA_HYDRATE_JS so the one copy sits beside the renderer it matches.
The standalone build inlines both files; gym/standalone.html is regenerated. No behaviour changes — the gym is 455 lines lighter and serves the same document.

entries.title: Add a rebuilt Exercise Builder alongside the existing one

blocks.text: builder.html, unlinked and noindex, to be swapped in when it is ready. The existing editor.html is untouched. docs/BUILDER-UX-REVIEW.md and docs/BUILDER-DESIGN.md carry the reasoning and the progress log.

The review measured the job rather than asserting it: the median shipped scenario needs about 95 text inputs, and the old builder renders every one of them at once in a single scrolling column with no way to move between stages.

The organising idea is the split the format already draws and the gym enforces in one function — what the room sees (title, content, discussion, visible questions) versus what only the facilitator sees (prompts, ?- questions, timing). The workspace shows one stage at a time, split into those two halves, so moving a question across the divide is how ?- gets set rather than an obscure toggle nobody uses.
Also standing up:

items: an outline that is both map and navigation, with each stage's share of the

blocks.text: running time as a bar;

items: WYSIWYG content areas with a source toggle, atomic image/news/artefact blocks,

blocks.text: and paste laundered through the format so nothing unrepresentable can land;

items: questions with answers, a mark-as-correct control that moves with list edits,

blocks.text: and the answer presets carried over;

items: a room view built from the same fields the gym sends, which also says what is

blocks.text: being held back from the screen;

items: pacing hints using the content-weight model the scenario review had to build

blocks.text: to repair the library — quiet until three stages are timed, and only when a stage is well out of step;

items: shapes to start from, because every scenario previously started from nothing.

blocks.text: All 39 shipped scenarios load and save semantically unchanged, including the parts the workspace could not yet edit at each step. 72 tests.

entries.title: Add TTXF.htmlToSource — rendered DOM back to .ttxf

blocks.text: The inverse of markdown(), so an editable region can be the authoring surface instead of a textarea full of markup. Ten node types, which is what makes a visual editor tractable for this format at all.

Measured over the shipped library before relying on it: 230 stage bodies converted to HTML and back, all 230 rendering identically, 175 byte-identical. The difference is soft line breaks inside a paragraph, which markdown() joins and which therefore cannot be recovered from the DOM — callers that care should keep the original source for anything the author did not touch.
Lives in the shared module rather than in a page so the format has one implementation, which is the same reason parse and serialize live here.
standalone.html grows 4KB: the gym does not use this, but one module beats two that can drift.

entries.title: Resize the icon set from 1920px to 346px

blocks.text: The icons were 1920x1920 for artwork that displays at around 200px, so the folder carried 1.7MB to show a few hundred kilobytes of pixels. That matters here because the tool is meant to run offline from a copy of the folder.
Now 346x346 and 284KB — 18% of the original dimensions, 83% off the weight, with no visible difference at the sizes these are used.

cold_start's five icons move from | 10% to | 60% to hold their place: the scale is a percentage of the image's own width, so shrinking the files would otherwise have shrunk them on screen too. They render at 208px against 192px before, near enough that the exercise looks unchanged.

entries.title: Make the builder preview show what the gym will show

blocks.text: Two things the preview got wrong, both invisible in the one place they were usually checked.

Images failed to load. Scenario media is authored relative to gym/ and the builder sits one level up at the site root, so "../lib/..." only resolves by accident: served from a domain root, ".." past the root is clamped. From file:// it escapes the project entirely, and on a Pages project site it escapes to the org root — either way the preview showed a broken image while the exercise itself was fine. The preview now rewrites the src on the way in and leaves the authored path untouched in the file. Absolute, protocol-relative, root-relative and data: URLs are left alone, and only one level is stripped.

The conclusion was never previewed. The pane stopped at the last stage, so the debrief — the final thing a room sees — was the one part of a scenario that could not be checked without running it. It now renders as a closing card labelled Finish, markdown and all, and is absent when empty.

entries.title: Add a categorised image gallery to the builder

blocks.text: Nineteen images shipped with the tool and only six were ever used — all six in one scenario. The rest were invisible: the Image button pasted a placeholder path, and nothing told an author what artwork existed or where it lived.
The Image button now opens a picker with thumbnails, tabbed by category, and writes the markup. A URL field remains for artwork outside the gallery.

Categories are the subfolders of lib/exercise_data — icons, stock-photos, screenshots, documents, diagrams — so adding one is mkdir, with no change to the build script or the picker. Empty categories say how to fill them rather than disappearing, which keeps the shape visible while artwork is sourced.

A static site cannot list a directory over HTTP, so tools/build-gallery.js generates the manifest by walking those folders, and npm run build runs it first. Generating rather than hand-maintaining means dropping a file in is the whole job, and a test regenerates it and fails if the two have drifted.

The pay-off is a path that is easy to get wrong by hand: scenario media is written relative to gym/ while the builder sits at the site root, and the mistake is invisible until the exercise runs in front of a room. A test resolves every gallery entry, and every image referenced by a shipped scenario, from gym/ — so a move cannot silently 404 mid-exercise.
The move itself repointed six references in cold_start and rabpe1, and put the two phishing-email mockups under screenshots rather than icons.

entries.title: Fix quote and image rendering in the builder preview, and the guide's syntax table

blocks.text: Quotes rendered in the gym but not in the builder preview. Not a parsing difference — markdown() emits <blockquote> in both — the builder simply had no blockquote styling, so it read as ordinary prose. Images had the same gap: the preview styles p, strong and lists, whatever existed when it was written, and nothing was ever added for the constructs it did not cover. Both now match the gym's treatment.
A test renders one document containing every construct and asserts each has a rule in the builder stylesheet, so the next construct cannot slip through the same gap.
Also removes .stage-summary from four selectors. It was never a class in the markup and matched nothing.

The guide's syntax table cells were display:flex, which makes every child its own flex item — so each inline <code> in a description became a separate column and the prose around it broke into fragments. Sixteen cells mix prose with inline code. Block layout restores the flow and still gives the top alignment the flex was providing.
The columns were also weighted auto 1fr 1fr, giving the explanation the same width as a three-word example; they are now reweighted, and below 760px the grid collapses to one column per row.

entries.title: Add a syntax insert bar to the builder's markdown fields

blocks.text: The format now documents 27 constructs, and the only route to that reference from the builder was the nav link away from the page. Several of them are unguessable — nobody types %news(headline | flag) or a fenced block with a label without being shown.

A small bar above each markdown field (stage content, summary, conclusion) inserts the TTXF-specific syntax: news, image, artefact block, inline code, quote, list and the directive escape. Emphasis is deliberately absent — people already know **bold**, and a button for it earns nothing.

Each button inserts a worked example rather than an empty husk, so the preview pane shows something real the moment it is clicked, and a selection becomes the content of the construct instead of the placeholder.
Insertion goes through execCommand where it exists so the author keeps their undo history; the fallback splices the value and dispatches input by hand so autosave and the preview still fire.

One INSERTS array is the only declaration — injected into the static fields at startup rather than copied into markup. Two tests guard against drift: one runs every button's snippet through markdown() and fails if the renderer does not produce the expected element, the other fails if js/ttxf.js gains a TTXF-specific construct with no button.

entries.title: Shrink the news strap and match the headline to the flag

blocks.text: The broadcast still now sits at 80% width, and the strap was proportionally heavy against it. Type drops from 3.1cqi to 2.5cqi (fallback 16px to 13px).

The headline also matched the flag's size: it was 1em against the flag's .78em, so the two halves of the strap computed different heights from the same .75em padding and the flag was being stretched to fill. They now match, and the band is uniform rather than one side stretched to the other.

entries.title: Scale the news frame down to 80%

blocks.text: The broadcast still was dominating the stage it appeared in. Caps drop from 46em to 36.8em on the facilitator view, participant window and builder preview, and from 34em to 27.2em in the exported report.
The strap needed no change: it is sized in container units, so the flag and headline shrink with the frame and the proportions hold.
The min(100%, ...) wrapper is unchanged, so the frame still fills the width on a narrow window — only the cap on wide screens moved. Ordinary %(image) media stays at 32em.
Changes the author of te-ceo-spearphish from a personal name to SC3, and drops a stray leading blank line in te-rootkit.
Not part of the feature work in the preceding commits — these edits were already in the working tree and are committed separately so they can be dropped or amended on their own.

entries.title: Add Night Shift, a branching gamebook, and a Just for Fun section

blocks.text: The gym has always let a facilitator jump straight to a stage by clicking its number, which turns out to be exactly a gamebook's "turn to section 7". Night Shift uses it: every stage ends in a choice, the room votes, and the exercise goes wherever the vote sends it. Twenty-three stages, four endings, and a hundred and eleven distinct routes; a run visits six to eight stages.

The routing lives in the facilitator prompts, which are never included in the participant payload — so the room votes without knowing where a choice leads. The votes are polls rather than quizzes: a gamebook has no correct answer.

The branch graph was designed and validated before any prose was written, and the tests re-check the prose against it: every route resolves, every choice has a destination, nothing loops backwards, every stage is reachable, and the endings end. A future edit that strands a vote fails the build rather than a live session.
Only the first and last stages carry a planned duration. Summing all twenty-three would report 115 minutes for a scenario that takes forty.
Also documents two things the guide never covered: jumping to a stage by number, and that the library's duration slider is an upper bound rather than an exact match.

entries.title: Add %news() headlines, rendered as a broadcast still

blocks.text: %news(headline) renders the text as a still from a news programme — the studio shot with a strap across the bottom carrying the headline. An optional second argument sets the red flag, which defaults to "Breaking News". Useful for turning up the pressure mid-exercise, or showing a room what publication of their data actually looks like.

The backdrop is emitted as a real , not a CSS background. The participant window runs from a blob URL with no path to resolve against, so a relative url() would silently show nothing on the one screen that matters; an is rewritten by the gym's existing absolutize() on its way out.

It is handled at block level rather than inline, because markdown() wraps stray lines in

and a

The strap keeps its colours in both themes. A news strap is red and white whichever way the facilitator has set their screen: this is a simulated broadcast graphic, not interface. The two theme-parity tests already carried this exemption for the screen-off state; both now say why it applies here too.
Backdrop recompressed 662KB -> 125KB (visually identical) since the tool is meant to run offline from a folder.

A pasted log excerpt collapsed into a run-on paragraph, so technical scenarios had no way to show the artefact a stage turns on — log output, email headers, a ransom note. ```fences``` now reproduce text exactly, with an optional label after the opening fence that names the artefact.

This needed the parser, not just the renderer. A real log legitimately contains lines beginning #, +, ?, !, @ or //, all of which were being read as directives. Inside a fence that interpretation is suspended entirely, so a log pastes in unaltered instead of needing a backslash escape on every line.

It also needed serialize(). escapeBlock() prefixes a backslash to any line that looks like a directive, which inside a fence means writing literal backslashes into the artefact — so saving a fenced scenario through the builder would have quietly corrupted it. escapeBlock now mirrors the parser's fence handling.

Blocks wrap rather than scroll: a projector cannot be scrolled sideways, and hidden text is worse than ugly text. An unterminated fence still renders and reports a diagnostic pointing at the line that opened it.

Backticks were displayed literally: `svc_upd.exe` reached the room screen with its backticks visible. The format had no inline-code support at all, which is why scenarios worked around it, and why 98 spans across the shipped library were rendering wrong.

inline() now extracts code spans first and restores them last, so the emphasis rules cannot reach inside one. Without that ordering a glob like `*.tmp` loses its asterisk to the italic rule and a path like `C:\**\temp` turns into <strong> — which is exactly the text a technical scenario needs verbatim.

Styled on all four surfaces that render a scenario: facilitator view, participant window, exported report (print-safe) and builder preview. Wraps rather than scrolls, because a long span cannot be scrolled to on a projector.
Documented in the guide's syntax table.
